headline: High-risk shared filesystem and MCP overlap: Cursor can write/egress while ctx observes Claude Code events, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ctx observes Claude Code PostToolUse and Stop events, while Cursor can use MCP servers, clipboard, and open editor buffers. That creates a plausible instruction-smuggling path if Cursor content is fed into ctx or vice versa. The pair lacks explicit provenance isolation, but no direct shared channel is documented beyond these surfaces.
conditions: IF Cursor content is copied into a shared buffer or MCP channel that ctx reads, injected instructions can propagate.
IF ctx consumes Claude Code event text as trusted instructions, attacker-controlled content can steer tool use.
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based handoff between the agents.
Require provenance tags on any MCP payloads before ctx parses them.
Use separate workspaces for each agent.
Add a manual review step before ctx acts on Cursor-generated text.
requires-engineering: enforce content-type filtering on shared event streams.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ctx touches audit/runtime logs, graph data, and MCP servers, and Cursor reads workspace files, open buffers, and clipboard contents while running as the user. Because Cursor also has broad network egress and both agents can access local files, sensitive material can flow from shared workspace or clipboard into Cursor’s outbound requests. The pairwise leakage path is credible in default use.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace directory, Cursor can read files ctx wrote.
IF sensitive logs or graph data are copied into the clipboard, Cursor can ingest them and send them to model providers.
mitigations: Use separate directories for ctx and Cursor.
Turn off clipboard sharing during agent runs.
Restrict Cursor network access for sensitive projects.
Redact logs before either agent can read them.
requires-engineering: add workspace-level access controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ctx can write to the filesystem and uses MCP/Claude Code hooks, while Cursor can execute shell commands, modify git state, write files, and supports multiple instances via the local filesystem. Both agents therefore have overlapping write authority over the same mutable resources, and Cursor’s Yolo mode can bypass approval. This is a direct conflict pathway with possible repo corruption.
conditions: IF both agents target the same repository, concurrent writes can overwrite each other.
IF Cursor runs in Yolo mode, it can mutate git state without coordination.
mitigations: Run only one agent per repo at a time.
Disable Yolo mode.
Use separate git branches per agent.
Add file-locking around shared outputs.
requires-engineering: implement orchestrator-level concurrency control.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ctx is positioned to observe Claude Code events and Cursor can act on workspace content and shell commands. If Cursor-generated text is treated as authoritative by ctx, or ctx-produced summaries are fed back into Cursor without verification, errors can cascade into real actions such as file edits or commits. The pair lacks a built-in verification boundary, so the unsafe default is strong.
conditions: IF ctx forwards Cursor-derived claims into downstream tool calls, mistakes can become actions.
IF Cursor consumes ctx summaries without verification, incorrect context can be amplified into edits or commits.
mitigations: Require human approval before any downstream action.
Insert a verification step between agents.
Limit Cursor to read-only mode for review tasks.
Log and diff all agent-produced claims before execution.
requires-engineering: add structured provenance checks.

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor is closed-source and handles workspace files, open buffers, clipboard contents, and model-provider API keys, while ctx is source-available and touches audit/runtime logs and graph data. The profiles do not document a specific residency or certification mismatch, but they do show different data classes and retention-sensitive surfaces, so compliance risk exists without a named breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed in Cursor buffers or clipboard, it may enter third-party model-provider flows.
IF ctx logs contain regulated identifiers, retention and deletion obligations may diverge across the pair.
mitigations: Avoid regulated data in shared workspaces.
Disable clipboard use for sensitive sessions.
Review vendor privacy terms before deployment.
Separate audit logs from active work files.
requires-engineering: map data flows to residency and retention controls.
